article.text:
The Cases and Controversies Requirements set the threshold for federal court jurisdiction: Standing ensures the plaintiff has a concrete, personal stake in the outcome; Ripeness requires the dispute to be sufficiently developed (not hypothetical); Mootness bars cases where the issue has already been resolved; the Political Question Doctrine excludes disputes better suited for the legislative or executive branches (e.g., impeachment proceedings).

Standing is the issue of whether the plaintiff is the proper party to bring a matter to the court for adjudication. The plaintiff must allege and prove that he or she has been injured or imminently will be injured (future injury). Plaintiffs only may assert injuries that they personally have suffered; plaintiffs seeking injunctive or declaratory relief must show a likelihood of future harm.

Disney wanted to build a ski resort in Mineral King Valley. Sierra Club, a membership corporation with a special interest in the conservation and sound maintenance of the national parks, game refuges, and forests of the country, brought this suit for a declaratory judgment and an injunction to restrain federal officials from approving an extensive skiing development in the Mineral King Valley because they believed that the project would cause irreparable harm to the public interest.

The case was brought up to Supreme Court in the end, and the Supreme Court ruled that Sierra Club had alleged no legal interest in the case, because they failed to allege that any of their members had ever used Mineral King. Then, they sent some of the members to walk in the Mineral King and amended their allegations accordingly. Then the court said that they had standing, since they had alleged a personally suffered injury.
article.reference: Standing asks whether the plaintiff is the proper party: the plaintiff must allege a concrete, personal injury, may assert only injuries personally suffered, and, for injunctive or declaratory relief, must show a likelihood of future harm. In the Mineral King case, the Sierra Club initially lacked standing because it failed to allege that any member had personally used the valley; after members visited and the complaint was amended to allege a personally suffered injury, standing existed.

comprehension.q: According to the article, what does the Mootness requirement bar?
options: Disputes better suited for the legislative or executive branches
Cases brought by plaintiffs with no personal stake in the outcome
Cases where the issue has already been resolved
Hypothetical disputes that are not yet sufficiently developed

comprehension.q: Why did the Supreme Court initially hold that the Sierra Club lacked standing?
options: Because the Sierra Club was not a membership corporation
Because it failed to allege that any of its members had personally used Mineral King
Because the ski resort had already been built
Because the case raised a political question

comprehension.q: What must a plaintiff seeking injunctive or declaratory relief show, according to the article?
options: That other taxpayers support the claim
That the defendant is a federal official
An injury actually suffered by a third party
